Chapter Seven: The Cost of Discipleship—Rediscovering Sacrifice in a Self-Centered Age.
Have you ever noticed how much our world celebrates comfort and convenience? These days, the idea of real sacrifice almost feels out of place—maybe even a little scary. But for generations, faith wasn’t just about what people hoped to receive. It was defined by what they were willing to give up.
Picture this: a young couple, freshly married and full of hope, dreaming of a life that checks all the boxes. They want to follow God, but they also crave the good life—a cozy home, thriving careers, maybe even a bit of admiration from their friends. At first, it seems like they can have it all. But as their faith grows deeper, there’s this gentle pull, almost like a whisper, inviting them to something greater.
It starts with the little things. Maybe they give up a weekend to volunteer at a shelter. Or they choose honesty at work—even when it means missing out on a promotion. They find themselves saying no to parties or activities that just don’t fit their values anymore. Each choice stings a little…it feels like saying goodbye to some part of themselves.
But then something surprising happens. The more they let go, the more alive they feel. Instead of shrinking, their lives seem to grow richer.
Most of us don’t even realize how much we’re shaped by chasing comfort. We’re told happiness is about getting what we want, exactly when we want it. But the old stories of faith flip that idea upside down. They say real joy comes, not from self-fulfillment, but from self-giving.
For this couple, the journey isn’t glamorous. They face confusion from friends, pressure from family, and plenty of doubts along the way. Yet through every challenge, they discover a love and purpose so much deeper than before. Their marriage grows stronger, friendships become more meaningful, and their faith turns resilient.
It becomes clear: discipleship costs something. But the cost? It’s absolutely worth it.
If the church wants to stand strong against our self-obsessed culture, it needs to remember how beautiful sacrifice can be. That means learning to say no to ourselves, putting others first, and trusting that God’s way—even when it’s tough—offers more than anything the world can promise.
And here’s something to really take to heart: sacrifice isn’t about earning God’s love or proving ourselves. It’s about letting go of lesser things, so we can open our hands to something truly greater. In a culture that’s all about self, choosing to lay down your life for others…that’s the most radical—and rewarding—act of all.
